article_title: An Economist on ELECTRICITY IN DOMESTIC ECONOMY

brief_context: Refers to where coal is burnt for domestic heating.
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE JANUARY, 1953

COAL USED FOR DOMESTIC HEATING (Tons)

DOMESTIC FIRES
38,000,000

ELECTRIC HEATING
4,000,000

WHERE IS THE GREATER SCOPE FOR SAVING? COMFORT HEATING

Something like a third of all the coal in this country is burnt to warm houses, the majority of that fuel going to heat the bricks and mortar or warm the air in the house—and the air that goes out of it through flues, ventilators and windows—and only incidentally and at the cost of enormous waste does it warm the people inside. Electricity gives heat as, when and where wanted to provide human comfort, and therefore “comfort heating ” more aptly describes electricity's role than does “house warming ” or “space heating.”

LUXURY OR NECESSITY?

brief_context: Refers to fuel-using habits of households in Britain.
brief_extract: Some part of the rapid post-war increase must be regarded as overtaking arrears of development which would have taken place much earlier but for the war. brief_context: Mentioned regarding development in the use of power.
brief_extract:
SANDERS presented it as part of the larger picture of the national economy
NO one seriously questions that the nation needs very much more electricity than it has today. The American worker has at his disposal something like three times the power available to the British worker, and unless means can be found not merely to bridge the gap but to keep pace with the extraordinary rapid development in the use of power which is going on in America and in other countries, then our chances of survival as a first-rate industrial power are slender indeed. Our population is unlikely to increase very much above the present 50 millions and the proportion of old people will steadily rise.

brief_context: Reference to the reliable construction of British electrical apparatus.
article_title: TOWARDS PERFECTION - a new E.A.W. Survey
brief_extract:
The Report shows the growing
realisation by the housewife of
what the electrical engineer and
designer have to offer her. The
manufacturers have accepted the
Report with interest, as the large
measure of satisfaction expressed
is a testimony to the reliable con-
struction of British electrical ap-
paratus, and guidance is given in
considering future designs. Long Life

The Report affords evidence
of the long life of well-chosen
electrical apparatus, much of
which has required no repairs at
all, e.g., the 30-years-old iron; the
25-years-old wash boiler; the 24-
years-old cooker; the 20-years-old
washing machine and water
heater of the same age; the 128
fires in the survey in use over 20
years, and the 100 refrigerators
used for over 10 years, as well as
the 40-years-old bowl fire requir-
ing only one new element and re-
plating; the 37-years-old kettle
with one new element and new
flex; and the 30-years-old vacuum
cleaner with an occasional new
belt.

brief_context: Place where Prince Charles gave a State banquet
brief_extract: Royal menus of a by-gone age strike one now as oversumptuous. For example, in 1761, a Royal City Banquet given in honour of George III and his Queen consisted of four services for the Royal family, each containing about ten dishes, and at a State banquet given by Prince Charles of Hohenlohe Kirchberg on 18th March, 1771, forty-eight separate dishes were served. The individual was not, however, expected to eat something of everything but to make a selection out of the total offered.

brief_context: Mentioned in the book title 'Life in Shakespeare's England'
brief_extract:
We may be sure that the Coronation meal of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II will combine appreciation of good food with restraint and good taste. It would be interesting to know what meal was served at the Coronation of Queen Elizabeth I, but as the menu is not to hand, we may glance instead at a dish of that period taken from Dover Wilson’s “Life in Shakespeare’s England.”

An Elizabethan Mince-Pie

“Take a leg of mutton and cut the best of the best flesh from the bone, and parboil it well: then put to it three pound of the best mutton suet, and shred it very small: then spread it abroad, and season it with pepper and salt, cloves and mace: then put in good store of currants, great raisins and prunes, clean washed and picked, a few dates sliced, and some orange-pills sliced: then being all well mixed together, put it into a coffin*, or into divers coffins, and so bake them: and when they are served up, open the lids, and strew store of sugar on the top of the meat, and upon the lid. And in this sort you may also bake beef or veal; only the beef would not be parboiled, and the veal will ask a double quantity of suet.”

Gervase Markham, The English Hus-Wife, 1623 (2nd Ed.)

Nearer to our own day and but a brief half century away was the déjeuner for the Coronation of King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra on 9th August, 1902.

THE ELECTRICAL AGE APRIL, 1953
Nechako River so that it now flows down to the Tahtsa Lake through a chain of lakes, creating a reservoir 350 square miles in area and 150 miles long, augmented by other rivers with fascinating Indian names, such as the Eutsuk and the Tetachuck. The best site for a power house was at Kemano, 10 miles away from the western end of the reservoir and 2,800 feet lower, barely above sea level. Twin tunnels, each 25 feet in diameter, were gauged out of the mountain to carry the vast volume of water to the turbines.

brief_context: Used as a height comparison for the penstocks.
brief_extract: The tunnels end in an artificial cavern 700 feet long, 80 feet wide and 118 feet high which forms the largest underground power station in the world. The water falls from the tunnel end through two "penstocks" (series of pipes) a height of 16 times that of Niagara. The tailrace runs from the turbines after use away to the Pacific 10 miles along the Kemano Valley and the Gardner Canal.

Contractors is an independent body directed by
representatives of important Associations inter-
ested in electrical installation work, including

Association of Consulting Engineers, The Elec-
trical Contractors’ Association of Scotland, The
Electrical Association for Women, The National
Farmers’ Union. Electrical Installation Contractors holding the
Certificate of the National Register have given
evidence of competency; their work is subject
to periodical inspection; they undertake to pay

appropriate trade agreement; and observe the
Regulations for the Electrical Equipment of
Buildings issued by the Institution of Electrical
Engineers.

In the control room was a fascinating array of panels, the whole station being controlled from a desk in this room by one man.

brief_context: Birthplace of the author in 1875.
brief_extract:
Suffice it to say I've had a few knocks as well as successes as I've travelled along the road for 78 years. Born in Westminster in 1875, I managed to get through a very delicate childhood and at the age of 17 was a weedy, anaemic type of girl—in the words of a youthful admirer, "looking like a delicate hot-house flower," but in the words of a practical aunt, "just a white-faced chit of a girl."

One day a brother some four years older said to me, "Why don't you buck up and do something instead of mooning around the place, why don't you get something to do." I snapped back, whilst angry tears filled my eyes—"What did he think I could do?" A very meagre education, owing to frequent illness, hadn't prepared me for any of the few avenues open to women in those days. Then he had a brain-wave.

He suggested it might be that thing called a "typewriter" which women had been using in America in newspaper offices, and evidently women were going to learn how to work it here, because there was a notice in the window "lady pupils taken." No harm I thought in poking my nose in and finding out what the new idea was, so next day I too peeped through the door and then boldly walked in and asked how much it would cost to learn. How little people realised in those days what a vast professional world was opening for thousands of English women!

brief_context: Location of John Cadbury's original cellar workshop.
brief_extract: The swimming baths are open to schools, and used for galas and various gatherings. It was interesting to learn that in March, 1824, young John Cadbury went into business as a tea and coffee dealer, and shortly afterwards experimented in grinding cocoa beans, his workroom being the cellar of his shop in Birmingham. He was joined by his brother Benjamin in 1847, and John's sons, Richard and George, took control in 1861.

location_standardised: Bourn stream, Bournville, Birmingham, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The stream beside which the Cadbury factory was built.
brief_extract: He was joined by his brother Benjamin in 1847, and John's sons, Richard and George, took control in 1861. In 1879 a new experiment was made in the building of a factory in the meadowland beside the Bourn stream, which with its 200 workers was the foundation of the now world-famous and the world's largest cocoa and chocolate factory. In passing it may be noted that the Aztecs of Mexico invented drinking chocolate—a drink for the great Emperor Montezuma who is said to "have enjoyed his 50 pitchers a day." The basic principles have not greatly changed in the past 500 years.

WE toured the Swansea Docks on a bright April day, being met at the main entrance by a representative of the Docks and Inland Waterways Executive. Across the river was the South Dock now used by fishing trawlers and coasting vessels as well as by craft which convey sand from the Bristol Channel.

brief_context: Geographic location of the Darland Hall all-electric farm.

brief_extract:
KEELING, Magazine Secretary, Chester

AT the kind invitation of Mr. Dudley Beck, the Chester Branch paid a most instructive visit to Darland Hall, his all-electric farm covering 400 acres on the English-Welsh border, where the labour force is considerably reduced owing to the extensive use of electricity for all operations. The farm supports a herd of about 400 pedigree Ayrshire dairy cattle, and the flow of milk from cow to consumer is as hygienic as modern production methods can procure.

brief_context: Location of the branch that visited the all-electric farm.
article_title: VISIT TO DARLAND HALL ALL-ELECTRIC FARM
brief_extract:
D. KEELING, Magazine Secretary, Chester

AT the kind invitation of Mr. Dudley Beck, the Chester Branch paid a most instructive visit to Darland Hall, his all-electric farm covering 400 acres on the English-Welsh border, where the labour force is considerably reduced owing to the extensive use of electricity for all operations.

brief_context: Destination for a young bull being exported from the farm.
brief_extract: In a herd of this type the care of young stock is of supreme importance, and electric heaters, which are thermostatically controlled, are suspended in the calf pens. The farmer's pride, his prize-winning Ayrshire bull, was to our relief well secured, and we also inspected a young bull which is shortly to be shipped under export licence to Alberta as part of the Dollar Drive. The exceptional cleanliness of the buildings and the demands of clean milk production could only be achieved by the use of unlimited quantities of fresh water, and this is provided by an artesian well which houses a submersible electric pump fixed at some 130 feet below ground level.

brief_context: Mentioned as the home country of a congress participant.
brief_extract: STOCKHOLM 1953 will long remain in the memories of the 1,300 women from the 20 affiliated countries of the International Federation of Business and Professional Women who attended the 6th Triennial Congress in July. They represented practically every profession open to women, from the well-known ones of law, medicine, education, engineering, journalism, advertising, accountancy, management in its many aspects, to the lesser-known professions such as that of grazier from Australia and mortician from the United States! They each took away with them a personal impression which accorded with their individual interests, whether these related to the treasures both historical and modern and the cultural activities of the progressive capital of a progressive State; to the city planning with its outstanding domestic and public architecture, its delightful statuary, fountains and gardens, and its lovely waterways; or to the opportunity to exchange ideas with women from other countries engaged in one’s own type of work in a different setting.

brief_extract:
It therefore makes a two-pronged attack on national prosperity, and the Committte of Enquiry is doubly welcomed. On 19th June a memorable debate took place in the House of Commons when the following Motion was adopted:
“That this House, noting the benefits already brought to many villages and farms by electricity, believes that the development of food production depends increasingly on the use of electric power in labour-saving farm equipment and convenient household amenities for those on the land, and urges that steps should be taken to develop the supply of electricity in rural areas as much and as fast as possible.”
Members of Parliament stressed the dual necessity of providing labour-saving apparatus for farm work and for the farm house, and perhaps the following quotations from different sides of the House will indicate the unanimity on the matter:
“Countrywomen, certainly the younger generation and I think the older generation too, will no longer put up with the primitive conditions set by candles and paraffin. A man's choice of jobs turns on his ability to give his wife modern facilities in her home — light at the turn of a switch, hot water on tap.”
“The farm worker will want an immersion water heater, a washing machine, an electric fire, an electric cooker, radio and television — not all at once, but in five or six years.”

article_title: Interesting Visits by E.A.W. Branches: TO EAST ANGLIAN DAILY TIMES COMPANY, LIMITED
brief_extract:
Bolton, Hon. Secretary, Ipswich

THE Ipswich Branch visited the head printing office in Ipswich of the company which publishes five news-papers—the East Anglian Daily Times, the Evening Star, the Felix-stowe Times, the Suffolk Chronicle and Mercury, and a sporting paper "The Green Un." Periodicals such as the East Anglian Magazine, cata-logues and stationery are also printed on the premises, and the colour printing processes were of special interest. All printing depends on electricity as the source of energy, gas only being used in the stereotyping foundry for melting down the "printer's lead," a mixture of lead, antimony and tin.

brief_context: Mentioned in the context of salts used in beer liquor.
brief_extract: It is first ground in the mills, and then mashed. After this it is added to the liquor, which consists of water in which five different salts, including Epsom, have been mixed. The mixture is then put into coppers and boiled.

brief_context: County mentioned as a source for hops.
brief_extract: Yeast is then added to the mixture and it is put to ferment and make more yeast. Hops from different parts of the country, including our own Kent, and some from abroad are added for flavour and as a preservative. An Excise Officer regularly visits the brewery to measure the amount of beer brewed and tests it for gravity in order to calculate the duty payable to the Customs and Excise Authorities.

brief_context: Mentioned as where devices to destroy bacteria were being developed.
brief_extract: Cooking would benefit by a new technique designed to cook food from the inside outwards, preserving the flavour and goodness — a technique already used to temper metals. Devices to destroy bacteria in the atmosphere were being developed in America, and would probably become general, and another branch of electrical science was being applied to the destruction of bacteria and impurities in waterworks. The preservation of food and the regeneration of the soil were other aspects of the question, and new materials and fabrics were prophesied.

article_title: A VISIT TO JOHN CROSSLEY'S CARPET FACTORY, HALIFAX
brief_extract: HORROCKS-TAYLOR, Magazine Secretary. The people of Halifax are justly proud of Dean Clough Mills, which is one of the largest carpet factories in the world, covering over 26 acres of ground and employing 2,000 personnel. Members of the Halifax and District Branch were conducted round parts of this large undertaking, which this year celebrates 150 years of carpet weaving.

location_standardised: Dean Clough, Halifax, West Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Location of a showroom visited to see finished carpets.
brief_extract: As the carpet passes over this drum the top of the corrugations are cut with a sharp blade and the result looks very much like plain tufted carpet and is hard wearing. One of our last looks at Dean Clough was in the showrooms, where the finished samples of many of the kinds of carpet we had seen being woven were displayed. We saw prayer rugs for the East, high quality Wiltons for cinemas and hotels, but the carpet which drew us all to it was in the 18th century Aubusson style on a cream ground with 43 pastel shades incorporated in the design which took six months to complete.
